Grade 12 Calculus · Lesson 1.390 min

Evaluating Limits Analytically

Evaluate limits exactly using substitution, limit laws, factoring, rationalizing, special trigonometric limits, and the Squeeze Theorem.

Choose a section to read or explore.

A guide to this lesson
ExplanationWorked exampleInteractive labPracticeCommon mistakeKey takeaway

Lesson overview

⌄

In the previous lesson, you estimated limits from tables and graphs. Now we calculate them exactly. The central habit is simple: substitute first. If the result is a real number, stop. If the result is 0/00/00/0, that is a signal to rewrite the expression — never the final answer.

Explanation
Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

  • Apply the limit laws and evaluate polynomial, rational, radical, composite, and trigonometric limits by direct substitution when valid.
  • Recognize that 0/00/00/0 is an indeterminate form, not an answer.
  • Rewrite an indeterminate quotient by factoring and cancelling a common factor.
  • Use the Factor Theorem, synthetic division, and polynomial long division when a polynomial factor is hidden.
  • Simplify complex rational expressions by building a common denominator.
  • Use a conjugate to rationalize a numerator or denominator containing radicals, and handle cube-root forms with the appropriate algebraic identity or substitution.
  • Compare left-hand and right-hand limits at piecewise, absolute-value, and greatest-integer breaking points.
  • Distinguish normal points from breaking points for greatest-integer functions.
  • Recognize endpoint/domain behavior and oscillating functions whose two-sided limit does not exist.
  • Apply the composite-function limit law when the outer function is continuous at the inner limit.
  • Determine a parameter by forcing the left-hand and right-hand limits to agree.
  • Evaluate trigonometric limits using lim⁡u→0sin⁡uu=1\lim_{u\to0}\frac{\sin u}{u}=1limu→0​usinu​=1 and lim⁡u→01−cos⁡uu=0\lim_{u\to0}\frac{1-\cos u}{u}=0limu→0​u1−cosu​=0.
  • Use the Squeeze Theorem when direct algebra does not expose the limit.
Definition

Indeterminate form

The form 0/00/00/0 does not tell us the value of a limit. It tells us that the numerator and denominator share behavior that may be hidden. Rewrite the function for nearby inputs, then evaluate the equivalent expression.

Mr. Marwan’s limit decision routine

⌄

Use this routine on every analytical limit. It keeps the work short and prevents you from choosing a complicated method too early.

Step 01

Substitute

Insert the target value before doing any algebra.

Step 02

Read the result

A finite number is the answer. A nonzero denominator is safe.

Step 03Do something

If 0/00/00/0: do something

Factor and cancel, rationalize, or use a trigonometric identity.

Step 04

Substitute again

Evaluate the simpler nearby expression and check the result.

Method chooser

Polynomial factors?
Factor and cancel.
Radicals?
Multiply by the conjugate.
Sine or cosine near zero?
Build a special limit.

Working:

Direct substitution and limit laws

⌄

Polynomials are continuous everywhere. Rational functions are continuous wherever their denominators are nonzero. Radicals and composite functions may also be evaluated by substitution when the substituted value lies in the domain.

lim⁡(f(x)g(x))\lim(f(x)g(x))lim(f(x)g(x))becomesLMLMLM

Dividing out: factor and cancel

⌄

When substitution gives 0/00/00/0 in a rational expression, look for a common factor. Cancelling is valid for nearby values where x≠cx\ne cx=c. A limit describes those nearby values, not the missing point itself.

a2−b2=(a−b)(a+b)a3−b3=(a−b)(a2+ab+b2)a^2-b^2=(a-b)(a+b)\qquad a^3-b^3=(a-b)(a^2+ab+b^2)a2−b2=(a−b)(a+b)a3−b3=(a−b)(a2+ab+b2)

Working:

Factor Theorem, synthetic division, and long division

⌄

When substitution gives 0/00/00/0 but a polynomial factor is hidden, use the Factor Theorem. If P(c)=0P(c)=0P(c)=0, then x−cx-cx−c is a factor. Synthetic division is efficient for a divisor of the form x−cx-cx−c; polynomial long division handles a general polynomial divisor.

P(x)=D(x)Q(x)+R(x)P(x)D(x)=Q(x)+R(x)D(x)P(x)=D(x)Q(x)+R(x)\qquad\frac{P(x)}{D(x)}=Q(x)+\frac{R(x)}{D(x)}P(x)=D(x)Q(x)+R(x)D(x)P(x)​=Q(x)+D(x)R(x)​
Interactive example · Synthetic division

27−21−60=00.\frac{27-21-6}{0}=\frac00.027−21−6​=00​.

2. Step 2 · Use the Factor Theorem

Because the numerator equals zero at x=3, x-3 is a factor.

3. Step 3 · Synthetic division

lim⁡x→3x3−7x−6x−3=lim⁡x→3(x−3)(x2+3x+2)x−3.\lim_{x\to3}\frac{x^3-7x-6}{x-3}=\lim_{x\to3}\frac{(x-3)(x^2+3x+2)}{x-3}.limx→3​x−3x3−7x−6​=limx→3​x−3(x−3)(x2+3x+2)​.

4. Step 4 · Cancel the common factor

lim⁡x→3(x−3)(x2+3x+2)x−3=lim⁡x→3(x2+3x+2),x≠3.\lim_{x\to3}\frac{(x-3)(x^2+3x+2)}{x-3}=\lim_{x\to3}(x^2+3x+2),\qquad x\ne3.limx→3​x−3(x−3)(x2+3x+2)​=limx→3​(x2+3x+2),x=3.

5. Step 5 · Substitute again

lim⁡x→3(x2+3x+2)=20.\lim_{x\to3}(x^2+3x+2)=20.limx→3​(x2+3x+2)=20.

8+4−8−44−4=00.\frac{8+4-8-4}{4-4}=\frac00.4−48+4−8−4​=00​.

2. Step 2 · Choose the division tool

The divisor is quadratic, so organize the work as polynomial long division: dividend, divisor, quotient, and remainder.

3. Step 3 · Divide

lim⁡x→2x3+x2−4x−4x2−4=lim⁡x→2(x2−4)(x+1)x2−4.\lim_{x\to2}\frac{x^3+x^2-4x-4}{x^2-4}=\lim_{x\to2}\frac{(x^2-4)(x+1)}{x^2-4}.limx→2​x2−4x3+x2−4x−4​=limx→2​x2−4(x2−4)(x+1)​.

lim⁡x→2x3+x2−4x−4x2−4=lim⁡x→2(x+1),x≠±2.\lim_{x\to2}\frac{x^3+x^2-4x-4}{x^2-4}=\lim_{x\to2}(x+1),\qquad x\ne\pm2.limx→2​x2−4x3+x2−4x−4​=limx→2​(x+1),x=±2.

5. Step 5 · Substitute again

lim⁡x→2(x+1)=3.\lim_{x\to2}(x+1)=3.x→2lim​(x+1)=3.
Common mistake. Synthetic division applies directly to a linear divisor of the form x−cx-cx−c. Do not force it onto a higher-degree divisor.

Working:

Rationalizing technique

⌄

If 0/00/00/0 comes from a square root, multiply by the conjugate. The product(a−b)(a+b)=a2−b2(a-b)(a+b)=a^2-b^2(a−b)(a+b)=a2−b2 removes the radical difference and usually reveals a factor that cancels.

Conjugate of u−a is u+a.\text{Conjugate of }\sqrt{u}-a\text{ is }\sqrt{u}+a.Conjugate of u​−a is u​+a.

Answer: Multiply by the conjugate\text{Multiply by the conjugate}Multiply by the conjugate

What is the conjugate of x+5−3\sqrt{x+5}-3x+5​−3?

  2. x−5+3\sqrt{x-5}+3x−5​+3

Answer: x+5+3\sqrt{x+5}+3x+5​+3

lim⁡x→4x+5−3x−4=lim⁡x→4x+5−9(x−4)(x+5+3).\lim_{x\to4}\frac{\sqrt{x+5}-3}{x-4}=\lim_{x\to4}\frac{x+5-9}{(x-4)(\sqrt{x+5}+3)}.limx→4​x−4x+5​−3​=limx→4​(x−4)(x+5​+3)x+5−9​.

Which factor cancels?

  2. x+5x+5x+5

Answer: x−4x-4x−4

lim⁡x→4x−4(x−4)(x+5+3)=lim⁡x→41x+5+3,x≠4.\lim_{x\to4}\frac{x-4}{(x-4)(\sqrt{x+5}+3)}=\lim_{x\to4}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+5}+3},\qquad x\ne4.limx→4​(x−4)(x+5​+3)x−4​=limx→4​x+5​+31​,x=4.

4. Step 4 · Evaluate

What is the final limit?

  1. 16\frac1661​
  2. 666
  3. 13\frac1331​

Answer: 16\frac1661​

lim⁡x→41x+5+3=16.\lim_{x\to4}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+5}+3}=\frac16.x→4lim​x+5​+31​=61​.
Common mistake. When multiplying by the conjugate, multiply both the numerator and denominator. You are multiplying by 111, so the value of the expression does not change.

Radical extensions: cube roots and substitution

⌄

The class notes extend the same routine beyond square-root conjugates. For cube-root differences, use the difference-of-cubes identity. When several fractional powers appear, introduce a substitution that converts them to ordinary polynomial powers.

a3−b3=(a−b)(a2+ab+b2)a^3-b^3=(a-b)(a^2+ab+b^2)a3−b3=(a−b)(a2+ab+b2)
